description: Shared regex fixtures (Paket 5) for the Rust engine (fancy-regex, cargo test) and the JS engine (native RegExp in FilterWorker, npm test). Operation: Filter per line (mode 'keep' or 'remove', defaults: mode=keep, caseSensitive=true, splitMatches=true). 'expected' is the filter result text or { "error": "invalidRegex" | "regexRuntime" }. Categories: 'same' = shared syntax, same result ('expected'); 'different' = accepted by both engines with different results; 'rustOnly' / 'jsOnly' = only one engine accepts the pattern. Every category except 'same' uses 'expectedRust' + 'expectedJs' and explains the difference in 'divergence'. Catastrophic backtracking is not part of these fixtures (the JS engine has no limit and would run for minutes): see the backtracking tests in src-tauri/src/text_processor.rs and tests/unit/worker-termination.test.ts. Paket 10 Phase B added the dialect differences R7 of docs/analyse/Paket10-PhaseA-Regex-Analyse.md (no compatibility translation). 'jsRuntimeDependent' { reason, otherJsResults } marks syntax whose JS result depends on the JS engine version (WebView2, WebKit, Node): the JS result must be the expectation or one of otherJsResults; no cross-version guarantee is claimed.

cases.name: lookbehind with alternatives of different (constant) length
only zero-width matches drop the line (splitMatches off)
\w is Unicode-aware only in Rust
cases.divergence: fancy-regex: \w is Unicode (letters, marks, digits, connector punctuation); JS RegExp without the 'u'/'v' flag: \w = [A-Za-z0-9_].

cases.name: \d is Unicode-aware only in Rust
cases.divergence: fancy-regex: \d = Unicode decimal digits (e.g. Arabic-Indic); JS: \d = [0-9] (also with the 'u' flag).

cases.name: \b around umlauts
cases.divergence: Word boundaries follow \w: Unicode in Rust, ASCII in JS (ü/ß are no word characters in JS, so 'e' starts a new word).

cases.name: \s and the byte order mark U+FEFF
cases.divergence: JS \s includes U+FEFF (ECMAScript WhiteSpace); Rust \s is Unicode White_Space, which does not contain U+FEFF.

cases.name: . matches a whole emoji only in Rust
cases.divergence: Rust matches Unicode scalar values; JS RegExp without the 'u' flag matches UTF-16 code units, so an emoji outside the BMP is two characters (surrogate pair).

cases.name: Unicode property escape \p{L}
cases.divergence: Rust: \p{L} = Unicode letters. JS without the 'u' flag: '\p' is an identity escape, the pattern means the literal text 'p{L}' (no error!).

cases.name: \A anchor
cases.divergence: Rust: \A = start of the text (here: of the line). JS without the 'u' flag: '\A' is the literal letter 'A'.

cases.name: \z anchor
cases.divergence: Rust: \z = end of the text (here: of the line). JS without the 'u' flag: '\z' is the literal letter 'z', the pattern means 'zz' or 'az'.

cases.name: \x{...} hex escape
cases.divergence: Rust: \x{41} = 'A'. JS without the 'u' flag: '\x' is the letter 'x' repeated 41 times.

cases.name: quantifier {,n}
cases.divergence: Rust: {,2} = {0,2}. JS: '{,2}' is not a quantifier and matches literally.

cases.name: POSIX character class [[:alpha:]]
cases.divergence: Rust: [[:alpha:]] = ASCII letters. JS: '[[:alpha:]' is a class of the characters '[', ':', 'a', 'l', 'p', 'h' followed by a literal ']'.

cases.name: case-insensitive Kelvin sign
cases.divergence: Rust (?i) uses Unicode simple case folding (k ~ K ~ Kelvin sign U+212A); JS 'i' without 'u' only compares toUpperCase() results.

cases.name: case-insensitive ß and capital ẞ
cases.divergence: Rust (?i): ß and ẞ (U+1E9E) are case variants. JS 'i' without 'u': 'ß'.toUpperCase() is 'SS', so ß only matches itself.

cases.name: case-insensitive backreference
cases.divergence: fancy-regex compares backreferences case-sensitively even under (?i); JS compares them case-insensitively with the 'i' flag.

cases.name: empty match directly after a non-empty match
cases.divergence: Rust's match iterator skips an empty match that starts where the previous match ended (matches at 0, 1..4, 5); JS matchAll reports it (0, 1..4, 4, 5).

cases.name: inline flag (?i)
cases.divergence: Inline flags (?i), (?m), (?s), (?x) at group level are Rust syntax. JS only knows modifier groups (?i:...) (ES2025, engine-dependent).

cases.name: Python-style named group (?P<name>...) and (?P=name)
cases.divergence: JS only supports (?<name>...) and \k<name>.

cases.name: atomic group (?>...)
cases.divergence: Atomic groups are a fancy-regex feature; JS has none.

cases.name: possessive quantifier
cases.divergence: Possessive quantifiers are a fancy-regex feature; in JS '++' is 'Nothing to repeat'.

cases.name: variable-length lookbehind
cases.divergence: fancy-regex only allows lookbehinds of constant length (alternatives may differ); JS allows any lookbehind.

cases.name: empty negated class [^]
cases.divergence: JS: [^] matches any character; Rust rejects the unclosed class.

cases.name: control escape \cI
cases.divergence: JS: \cI = TAB (control character escape); fancy-regex has no \c escape.

cases.name: \h is a hex digit only in Rust
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: fancy-regex \h = hex digit [0-9A-Fa-f]; JS without the u flag treats the unknown escape \h as the letter h.

cases.name: \u{...} code point escape only in Rust
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: \u{1F600} is U+1F600 in fancy-regex; JS without the u flag reads it as the letter u followed by the literal text {1F600}.

cases.name: \0 matches NUL only in JS
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: JS \0 is the NUL character; fancy-regex accepts \0 but it does not match NUL (no error, silently no match).

cases.name: . and the line separator U+2028
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: JS . excludes the ECMAScript line terminators U+2028/U+2029 (also without the m flag); fancy-regex . only excludes \n.

cases.name: . and the paragraph separator U+2029
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: like U+2028, JS . excludes U+2029.

cases.name: \s and the next line character U+0085
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: Rust \s is Unicode White_Space (contains U+0085); JS \s does not contain U+0085 (but U+FEFF, see above).

cases.name: \Z is a literal Z in JS
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: fancy-regex rejects the escape \Z; JS without the u flag treats \Z as the letter Z (no end anchor).

cases.name: \1 without a capture group
cases.divergence: Paket 10 R7: fancy-regex rejects a backreference to a missing group; JS (Annex B) reads \1 as the octal escape U+0001.

cases.name: $ before U+2028 inside a line (Filter flag g, no m)
modifier group (?i:...) depends on the JS runtime

jsRuntimeDependent.reason: Paket 10 R7: RegExp modifiers (?i:...) exist since V8 12.5 (Chrome/Edge/WebView2 125, Node 23). Older runtimes, e.g. an old WebView2 or Node 22, reject the pattern; WebKitGTK/WKWebView follow their own release.
